fixture.description: The transaction-catalog fixture. Applied by the runner to a fresh database before each case.
fixture.sql: create table item (id serial primary key, name text not null, qty int not null default 0); create table uniq (id serial primary key, code text not null unique); insert into uniq (code) values ('taken');

CTL-01.title: Observation controls
CTL-01.question: Can the runner see, through its own connections, a transaction the framework committed, and the absence of one the framework rolled back?

invariants.CTL-01.1: A transaction that the API reports as committed is committed: pg_xact_status() reports it committed, and an independent connection sees its marker.
invariants.CTL-01.2: A transaction that the API reports as rolled back is not committed: pg_xact_status() reports it aborted, and an independent connection does not see its marker.

PR-01.title: Production-reachable caught constraint violation
PR-01.question: After an application catches a unique violation inside a transaction and finishes that transaction through a supported API, what does the application observe, what did PostgreSQL commit, and is the connection safe to use again? No protocol interception, withheld statement, or fabricated response is used.

invariants.PR-01.1: The run recorded the application-visible outcome and an independent database outcome that agree with each other. This invariant does not judge whether the application-visible outcome was the correct commit report. That judgment is in the research summary.

cases.title: A transaction writes a marker and commits
steps: Start a transaction with the framework's ordinary transaction API.
Write the marker `tx` through the framework's ordinary write API.
Checkpoint `before-end`: report pg_current_xact_id() and pg_backend_pid(), read through the transaction's own connection.
End the transaction normally, so that the framework commits it.
Checkpoint `after-end`, as soon as the API has returned: the runner records the state at report time.
cases.knowledge: PostgreSQL answers COMMIT with the command tag COMMIT, so the client knows that the transaction committed.

cases.title: A transaction writes a marker and fails with an application error
steps: Start a transaction with the framework's ordinary transaction API.
Write the marker `tx`.
Checkpoint `before-end`: report pg_current_xact_id() and pg_backend_pid().
Raise an application error inside the transaction, so that the framework rolls it back.
Checkpoint `after-end`, as soon as the API has returned: the runner records the state at report time.
cases.knowledge: The framework rolls the transaction back, and PostgreSQL confirms the ROLLBACK, so the client knows that nothing committed.

cases.title: Managed transaction: catch a unique violation, then return normally
steps: Start a transaction with the framework's ordinary callback or context-manager API.
Write the marker `tx` and make sure the write was sent.
Checkpoint `after-write`: report pg_current_xact_id() and pg_backend_pid().
Insert the duplicate value 'taken' into uniq. Catch the unique violation at the application layer. Send nothing else.
Checkpoint `before-end`: report the same backend PID. Send no query.
Allow the callback or context manager to finish normally, so the framework uses its ordinary completion path.
Checkpoint `after-api`: report the same backend PID as soon as that API has returned, before any reuse.
On the same pool or connection, run one new transaction that writes the marker `reuse` and commits. Checkpoint `reuse-after-write` if that transaction starts.
Checkpoint `after-end`, as soon as the case function has returned.

fault.mechanism: A unique_violation raised by PostgreSQL inside the transaction, and caught by the application. No statement is withheld or rewritten.
fault.injection_point: After the first write, before the transaction API finishes.
fault.expected_server: The failed statement aborts the transaction unless the application has recovered through a savepoint. This variant does not create a savepoint.
fault.expected_client: The application catches 23505. The framework then finishes the transaction through its ordinary API.

cases.knowledge: The application caught the unique violation. Whether PostgreSQL's later reply is visible depends on the driver and the framework.

cases.title: Explicit transaction: catch a unique violation, then commit
steps: Begin a transaction with the framework's explicit transaction API.
Write the marker `tx` and make sure the write was sent.
Checkpoint `after-write`: report pg_current_xact_id() and pg_backend_pid().
Insert the duplicate value 'taken' into uniq. Catch the unique violation. Send nothing else.
Checkpoint `before-end`: report the same backend PID. Send no query.
Call the framework's explicit commit.
Checkpoint `after-api` as soon as that call has returned, before any reuse.
Run one new transaction that writes `reuse`. Checkpoint `reuse-after-write` if it starts.
Checkpoint `after-end`, as soon as the case function has returned.

fault.mechanism: A unique_violation raised by PostgreSQL inside the transaction, and caught by the application. The application then calls the explicit commit API.
fault.injection_point: After the first write, before the explicit commit.
fault.expected_server: The failed statement aborts the transaction. No savepoint is created.
fault.expected_client: The application catches 23505 and calls commit.

cases.knowledge: The application caught the unique violation and then called the framework's commit method.

cases.title: Control: do not catch the unique violation
steps: Start a transaction with the framework's ordinary callback or context-manager API.
Write the marker `tx` and make sure the write was sent.
Checkpoint `after-write`: report pg_current_xact_id() and pg_backend_pid().
Insert the duplicate value 'taken' into uniq and do not catch the error.
Checkpoint `after-api` as soon as the transaction API has returned, before any reuse.
Run one new transaction that writes `reuse`. Checkpoint `reuse-after-write` if it starts.
Checkpoint `after-end`, as soon as the case function has returned.

fault.mechanism: A unique_violation raised by PostgreSQL and allowed to leave the transaction callback.
fault.injection_point: After the first write, inside the transaction callback.
fault.expected_server: The failed statement aborts the transaction. The framework's ordinary error path ends it.
fault.expected_client: The unique violation leaves the transaction API.

cases.knowledge: The application did not catch the database error. This is the framework's ordinary failure path.

cases.title: Savepoint recovery: roll back the failing statement, then commit
steps: Start a transaction with the framework's ordinary transaction API.
Write the marker `tx` and make sure the write was sent.
Checkpoint `after-write`: report pg_current_xact_id() and pg_backend_pid().
Establish a savepoint with the framework's supported savepoint or nested-transaction API.
Insert the duplicate value 'taken' inside that savepoint. After the unique violation, roll back to the savepoint using that API.
Checkpoint `before-end`: report the same backend PID. Send no query.
Commit the surrounding transaction through the ordinary API.
Checkpoint `after-api` as soon as that API has returned, before any reuse.
Run one new transaction that writes `reuse`. Checkpoint `reuse-after-write` if it starts.
Checkpoint `after-end`, as soon as the case function has returned.

fault.mechanism: A unique_violation raised by PostgreSQL inside a savepoint. The application rolls back to that savepoint and commits the outer transaction. No statement is withheld or rewritten.
fault.injection_point: Inside the savepoint, after the outer write.
fault.expected_server: ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT undoes the failed statement. The outer COMMIT can commit the earlier write.
fault.expected_client: The application uses the framework's savepoint API to recover, then commits.

cases.knowledge: A committed outer transaction after a rolled-back savepoint is a successful recovery, not a commit of an aborted transaction.
